summary:
Tanzania criminalises same-sex sexual conduct. The Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 provides a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for same-sex acts between men; section 138A treats "gross indecency" as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework.

The semi-autonomous jurisdiction of Zanzibar, governed by its own House of Representatives, runs a separate criminal statute. The Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 defines "gross indecency" broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute below 12, with under-18 and marriage distinctions) and provides penalties including three years' imprisonment. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine.

No same-sex relationship has legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania. A partner cannot be sponsored, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin through relationship status, and adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly.

On 9 June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as "horrendous" the attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo, who was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut. The UN called for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people and flagged possible violations of ICCPR Article 20 and the equality guarantees of Tanzania's Constitution under Article 13. This is the most recent documented instance of anti-trans violence in this inventory; no later instance is documented.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report "We Are Facing Extinction" documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment.

State action against LGBT people is documented with dates. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of promoting homosexuality, directly disrupting services. In 2018 a witch hunt against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture; the same year the Regional Commissioner of Dar es Salaam, Paul Makonda, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people. The Foreign Ministry said the crackdown lacked government support, and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid.

Earlier documentation establishes the pattern of custody abuse. A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report for Tanzania likewise details police custody abuse, lists discrimination based on sexual orientation among the country's problems, and describes the human rights record as poor.

Online information access is restricted. An OONI report published in 2024, "Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship", documents the blocking of LGBTIQ websites, LGBTIQ social networks and rights sites on the basis of OONI measurement data, evidencing state-directed online filtering that constrains LGBT access to information.

Freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. The 2018 broadcast content regulations bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; the online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Health policy contains non-discrimination language on sexual orientation. The 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, colour or sexual preference; the Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated.
tangentialFactors:
Tanzanian activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials including former president Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, who pushed persecution. Their public positions indicate that advocacy carries visible personal exposure.

The US State Department's 2013 report named security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C and lack of access to justice as the three most widespread problems in Tanzania, alongside discrimination based on sexual orientation and societal violence against persons with albinism. The ranking is by the report's own assessment and covers the country generally, not trans people specifically.

There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some places exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. An interview with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists published on 4 September 2020 documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy.

Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate with reportedly one million people infected, and the October 2017 deportation of HIV/AIDS group staff shows that service delivery for LGBT populations has been disrupted by enforcement action.
localsOnly:
Residents of Zanzibar are subject to the Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives and to Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934 as amended in 2004, which are separate from the mainland Penal Code framework and carry their own penalties, including three years' imprisonment for gross indecency and up to five years or a TSh 500,000 fine for sex between women.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania, so no partner can be sponsored, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly.

Resident access to healthcare is governed by the non-discrimination provisions of the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards, the Nursing and Midwifery (Practice) Regulations 2010 and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care, which require care regardless of sexual orientation. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated.

Media professionals remain bound by the Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals, which bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation, even though the 2018 online content regulations carrying a similar ban were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations.

Residents seeking LGBTIQ information online encounter state-directed filtering: the 2024 OONI report documents blocking of LGBTIQ websites, social networks and rights sites.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be retrieved; its underlying documentation of criminalisation, including the availability of life imprisonment, is carried here from the inventory's own description rather than from the live page.

Several enforcement and speech claims in this record derive from a Wikipedia article and its cited sources rather than from primary documents consulted directly; the underlying reports (2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition, the 2013 US State Department report, Amnesty International January 2024, OONI 2024) are named so they can be verified.

No trans-specific killing or violence rate for Tanzania appears in this inventory, and no general homicide rate is available for comparison, so no trans-specific rate can be stated. No survey of trans people specifically, with a stated period and category measured, is present; the 2020 interview covers LGBT activists generally and is dated to that year.

Whether the 2018 Dar es Salaam committee and the witch hunt it announced remain operational is unresolved in this inventory; the most recent documented instance of anti-trans violence here is the June 2024 attack on Mauzinde, and no later instance is documented. Whether the deferred legislation on same-sex relations has since been enacted is likewise unresolved.
